papers.title: Hedwig: Dynamic Autonomy for Coding Agents Under Local Oversight
papers.authors: Tanjal Shukla, K. J. Kevin Feng, Leijie Wang, Mohammad Rostami, Amy X. Zhang
papers.venue: ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems (CAIS 2026), demo; arXiv preprint arXiv:2605.11495
papers.cite_role: Closest predecessor: per-developer oversight policy learned across sessions
papers.summary: Hedwig is a CLI coding agent demo that adapts its autonomy from developer interaction traces rather than static permission settings or instruction files. Hard constraints sit alongside learned behavioral guidance. An online logistic regression over 13 action features, updated by SGD after each decision and persisted per repository, scores each proposed action into silent approval, flagged approval, or live check-in. Corrections are stored as text snippets and retrieved into prompts. A synthetic-persona evaluation against Claude Code with Auto Memory shows higher recall for a cautious persona but more false positives for a permissive one. There is no user study and no transfer evaluation, so the authors frame it as a proof of concept.
papers.what_is_learned: interaction policy (evolving natural-language guidelines governing autonomy/oversight)
papers.user_evidence: Developer approval/oversight decisions and feedback during coding sessions
papers.decisions_raw: act / confirm / defer (dynamic autonomy level, when to require approval)
papers.relation: This is nearly a direct USIL instance: a persistent, user-conditioned autonomy policy learned from approvals across sessions. Open questions: how well do the learned guidelines generalize to new task types, and how should they handle trust miscalibration after a costly error?
papers.closest_overlap: Hedwig learns a per-repository, evidence-driven check-in policy from developer approvals and denials, with coefficients persisted across sessions, so it directly instantiates a user-conditioned policy for when to confirm, act, or ask. It differs from USIL in that personalization is keyed to the repository, not an individual user, and it is shown only with synthetic personas.
papers.remaining_question: Does a per-repository check-in classifier trained on real developers' approvals transfer across repositories and tasks for the same developer, and can it separate genuine preference drift from noise, given the fixed threshold and no recency weighting?

papers.title: Towards Automating Data Access Permissions in AI Agents
papers.authors: Yuhao Wu, Ke Yang, Franziska Roesner, Tadayoshi Kohno, Ning Zhang, Umar Iqbal
papers.venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P) 2026
papers.cite_role: Per-user permission (confirm vs act) prediction from 1–4 examples
papers.summary: The paper proposes automating data-access permissions for AI agents with an assistant that learns each user's allow/deny preferences. A vignette study with 205 Prolific participants identifies the factors that shape permission decisions. A hybrid predictor combines o3-mini in-context learning on the user's own history and demographics with LightGCN collaborative filtering over other users. It reaches 85.1% accuracy overall and 94.4% at 25.9% coverage when only high-confidence predictions are automated and uncertain ones are deferred to the user. Accuracy improves with more history, but high-variance users are hard to predict. It is a proof of concept with no temporal evaluation and no external baselines.
papers.user_evidence: Past allow/deny permission decisions, demographics, self-reported privacy and AI attitudes, and other users' decisions (collaborative filtering)
papers.decisions_raw: confirm / act (auto-grant vs. ask the user for permission)
papers.relation: This is close to learning pi_u for confirm-vs-act from sparse approvals and rejections. Open question: does a predictor of offline decisions remain calibrated when deployed live, as preferences drift and the agent's own auto-decisions change what evidence the user gives?
papers.closest_overlap: The paper learns an individual user's procedural preference, namely whether to permit data access without asking, from that user's decision history, and routes low-confidence cases back to the user. This is close to a user-conditioned pi_u over act versus defer or ask, with per-user analysis of predictability [personalization][interaction_decisions].
papers.remaining_question: Do per-user permission-delegation preferences remain stable and transfer across sessions, tasks and real agent deployments, and can the confidence-based defer rule be learned per user, with drift handled, rather than set by a global threshold on vignette data?

papers.title: When Should Users Check? Modeling Confirmation Frequency in Multi-Step Agentic AI Tasks
papers.authors: Jieyu Zhou, Aryan Roy, Sneh Gupta, Daniel Weitekamp, Christopher J. MacLellan
papers.cite_role: Decision-theoretic confirmation frequency (population-level)
papers.summary: The paper asks when an agent should ask users to confirm intermediate steps in long multi-step agentic tasks. A formative study identifies a confirmation-diagnosis-correction-rollback (CDCR) pattern. The authors build a decision-theoretic dynamic-programming scheduler that places checkpoints to minimize expected user time. In a 48-participant within-subjects study against confirm-at-end, the scheduler cut completion time by 13.54% and was preferred by 81%. Gains were largest for early errors and slightly negative for late errors. Parameters are population-level and fixed. Personalization and online adaptation are explicitly deferred to future work, and time is the only cost modeled.
papers.relation: Directly models confirmation; open question is learning the schedule per user.
papers.closest_overlap: It directly addresses when an agent should ask for confirmation versus proceed autonomously in long-horizon tasks, which is the P3 decision USIL wants to personalize. It frames confirmation as a time-minimizing decision-theoretic schedule and shows an averaged-population version beating confirm-at-end by 13.54% with 81% preference [key_results][interaction_decisions]. It is a clean procedure_averaged baseline.
papers.remaining_question: Can the per-user timing and accuracy-belief parameters (confirmation time, diagnosis time, trust in the agent) be learned online from sparse real interaction history, and does a per-user checkpoint schedule beat this population-level one in longitudinal deployment, beyond time cost?

papers.title: Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents
papers.authors: K. J. Kevin Feng, David W. McDonald, Amy X. Zhang
papers.cite_role: Autonomy treated as a fixed design choice (the practice the position argues against)
papers.summary: This position paper proposes five levels of agent autonomy defined by the role the user plays: operator, collaborator, consultant, approver and observer. It treats autonomy as a design choice distinct from capability and environment. It sketches autonomy certificates for governance and assisted evaluations that assign a level from the minimum user involvement needed to reach a performance threshold. A running example illustrates each level, and open questions ask when an agent should consult or seek approval. There are no experiments, learning mechanisms or user data. Personalization appears only conceptually, as user-specified approval conditions and a possible L3 training period. It is useful as a vocabulary for procedure-level autonomy that is averaged across users.
papers.relation: Treats autonomy as a fixed design choice; USIL asks whether it should be learned per user and context.
papers.closest_overlap: Treats autonomy as a design decision about how the agent works, separate from capability. It defines levels in terms of when the agent consults, asks approval, or hands over control, which are the decisions USIL wants learned per user. L4 users specify approval conditions and L3 agents may need a training period to learn user expertise and preferences [personalization].
papers.remaining_question: How could the autonomy level, or the consult/approve boundary within a level, be learned and adjusted per user from approvals, takeovers and corrections over time, and could assisted evaluations be extended to measure individual-level calibration rather than a single agent-level certificate?

papers.title: Proactive Agent: Shifting LLM Agents from Reactive Responses to Active Assistance
papers.authors: Yaxi Lu, Shenzhi Yang, Cheng Qian, et al.

papers.title: Robot Behavior Personalization from Sparse User Feedback
papers.authors: Maithili Patel, Sonia Chernova
papers.venue: IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (DOI 10.1109/LRA.2025.3550833); arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.19219
papers.cite_role: Per-user assistance/autonomy mode from sparse feedback, transfers to new tasks
papers.summary: TAACo personalizes a household robot's manner of assistance (do now, do later, remind, or no action) from sparse verbal feedback. GPT-4 scores abstract concepts for each task, and a per-user transformer is trained on these scores plus state variables, with attention aligned to user explanations. In interviews with five older adults (173 tasks), TAACo reached 0.71 prediction accuracy with 40 samples and 0.74 explanation accuracy, beating few-shot GPT-4 and a rule-based baseline. It generalizes to held-out tasks within each user. It does not study temporal drift, cross-user transfer, or asking decisions, and the sample is small.
papers.user_evidence: Sparse user feedback on preferred assistance mode for household tasks
papers.decisions_raw: act / defer (do task autonomously, assist, or leave it to the user); explain (concept-based explanations)
papers.relation: This directly learns user-specific 'which steps to run autonomously' with cross-task transfer from sparse evidence. Remaining questions: does it adapt online to preference drift, and does the concept representation carry over to LLM agents working in software?
papers.closest_overlap: It learns per-user procedural preferences, meaning whether the robot acts now, acts later, reminds, or does nothing, from sparse verbal feedback from five older adults. It does so with person-specific models and transfers to held-out tasks. This is close to the procedure_individual cell, using abstract concepts as a user representation z_u.
papers.remaining_question: Can concept-based per-user adaptation preferences be learned online from implicit evidence (takeovers, corrections) and updated as preferences drift over sessions? Can they extend to decisions about when to ask or confirm, and can they transfer across users or to new contexts rather than only new tasks within one user's data?

papers.title: Training Proactive and Personalized LLM Agents
papers.authors: Weiwei Sun, Xuhui Zhou, Weihua Du, et al. (incl. Graham Neubig, Maarten Sap, Yiming Yang)
papers.cite_role: Closest predecessor: policies conditioned on given interaction preferences (UserVille)
papers.summary: The paper introduces UserVille, which turns static datasets into vague-prompt tasks with LLM user simulators holding hidden precise prompts and one of 20 interaction preferences. It also introduces PPP, a multi-objective RL method that jointly optimizes task productivity, proactivity (low user effort) and personalization (preference compliance). An agent trained on Seed-OSS-36B learns when to ask clarifying questions and how to phrase them, outperforming GPT-5 on average (+16.72), and generalizes to unseen preferences, other simulators and full SWE tasks. A 33-person user study partly confirms this but shows a sim-to-real effort gap. Personalization is preference-conditioned, not learned per user over time.
papers.user_evidence: simulated user answers to questions, user-centric feedback on preference adherence and effort, task outcome
papers.decisions_raw: ask, clarify, act (when to ask and how targeted the questions are; how to communicate)
papers.relation: Closest existing instance of training an interaction policy conditioned on user interaction preferences, but it conditions on a preference specified per episode by a simulator rather than learning it from an individual user's evidence across sessions.
papers.closest_overlap: PPP trains a single RL policy over ask-versus-act decisions and rewards adherence to 20 simulated users' interaction preferences (selection-only, JSON, language), so it evaluates procedural adaptation and generalization to 8 held-out preferences. This is the closest existing instance of learning how an agent interacts rather than only what it produces.
papers.remaining_question: Can PPP-style training be extended so the agent infers an individual user's interaction preferences from sparse, noisy, evolving evidence (edits, answers, takeovers) across sessions, instead of receiving one of 20 stated preferences, and does it still work with real users given the sim-to-real gap in effort estimation?

papers.summary: Learns shared-autonomy assistance from scratch by exploiting the fact that users repeat daily tasks. papers.user_evidence: Repeated teleoperation demonstrations by the same user

papers.title: Human-Robot Mutual Adaptation in Shared Autonomy
papers.cite_role: HRI line: mutual adaptation in shared autonomy
papers.summary: This paper proposes a human-robot mutual adaptation formalism for shared autonomy. A bounded-memory model of human adaptability (BAM) is embedded in a MOMDP with a disagreement penalty. The robot maintains a belief over each user's goal and adaptability α and decides whether to guide the user toward an optimal goal or comply with their preference. In a 51-participant table-clearing study, the mutual-adaptation robot raised team performance over one-way adaptation (following the user) while keeping trust higher than a no-adaptation baseline. Adaptation is within-task only, α is fixed, the model is hand-specified, and transfer is untested.
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P2;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.
papers.closest_overlap: The robot maintains a per-user belief over adaptability α and uses it to choose between steering the user toward a better goal and deferring to the user's preference. This is a per-user autonomy/deference policy [personalization][interaction_decisions]. It is close to USIL's pi_u over act and defer decisions, but it is inferred within a single task rather than learned across sessions.
papers.remaining_question: Can a per-user adaptability or compliance parameter like α be learned across sessions, allowed to drift over time, and transferred to new tasks, rather than fixed within one table-clearing task and hand-specified in the model?

papers.title: The Off-Switch Game
papers.authors: Dylan Hadfield-Menell, Anca Dragan, Pieter Abbeel, Stuart Russell
papers.cite_role: Formal deference under uncertainty
papers.summary: The Off-Switch Game is a one-shot game-theoretic analysis of why a rational agent would allow a human to switch it off. A robot that is uncertain about the human's utility, and treats the human's off-switch decision as evidence about that utility, has a positive incentive to defer. A robot with a fixed, known reward lacks this incentive unless the human is rational. For a noisily rational human, the incentive depends on a tradeoff between the robot's uncertainty and the human's suboptimality. The paper has no learning, personalization, temporal adaptation, or empirical evaluation. It is a formal foundation for deference and autonomy decisions relevant to P3.
papers.relation: Formal model of deference; USIL adds individual variation in desired oversight.
papers.closest_overlap: The paper formalizes when an agent should defer to a human rather than act, using uncertainty about the human's utility and treating the human's switch-off decision as evidence (Theorems 1-2, Corollary 1). This is a theoretical basis for the P3 question of when to defer or return control [interaction_decisions][key_results].
papers.remaining_question: How can off-switch-style deference incentives be extended from a single, population-level, one-shot game to a sequential setting where the agent learns a per-user belief over each user's preferences about oversight, using that user's approvals, rejections, and takeovers over time? The authors name sequential settings and model misspecification as future work [temporal_adaptation][limitations].

papers.title: Assistant or Actor? Student Trust, Control, and Delegation Regret When Using a General-Purpose AI Agent
papers.authors: Shiva Pochampally, Shengwei An, Yan Chen
papers.cite_role: Evidence: delegation regret when agents act beyond authorization
papers.summary: A within-subjects study of 20 AI-literate CS students used a general-purpose agent on five tasks that varied in privacy, stakes and reversibility. Trust was calibrated per task: it was lowest, and approval preference highest, for the email-sending task, where the agent acted without showing a preview. Participants often rated outputs as successful yet regretted that the agent had acted without authorization, which the authors name 'delegation regret'. They argue that irreversibility plus external visibility, not stakes alone, drives trust withdrawal, and they propose an agent management layer with user-specified autonomy levels. The study is small, uncounterbalanced and single-session, and it contains no personalization or learning.
papers.relation: Evidence that acting beyond authorization harms users even when outcomes are correct.
papers.closest_overlap: The paper shows that dissatisfaction with a general-purpose agent comes from acting beyond the user's authorization boundary, not from wrong output. It also finds that trust and approval preferences vary by task, with irreversibility and external visibility (the email-sending task T2) driving the need for confirmation. This directly motivates procedure-level evaluation and adaptive autonomy and confirmation, the core of USIL, though only at the population level [key_results][interaction_decisions].
papers.remaining_question: Do the confirmation and autonomy preferences found here (preview and approval before irreversible, externally visible actions such as email) vary systematically across individual users? If they do, can an agent learn them per user from approvals, rejections and takeovers over repeated sessions, rather than having users set autonomy levels by action type up front? The paper reports only group-level statistics from a single fixed-order session and an unevaluated proposal [personalization][temporal_adaptation].

papers.title: Collaborative Gym: A Framework for Enabling and Evaluating Human-Agent Collaboration
papers.authors: Yijia Shao, Vinay Samuel, Yucheng Jiang, John Yang, Diyi Yang
papers.cite_role: Collaboration-process evaluation without per-user adaptation
papers.summary: Co-Gym is an open framework for developing and evaluating LM agents that collaborate with humans, with dual control of task environments and non-turn-taking interaction. It supports simulated users (gpt-4o with hidden preferences) and real users (99 participants, 150 trajectories) across Travel Planning, Related Work, and Tabular Analysis. Prompted agents (autonomous, collaborative, and situational-planning) are compared on delivery, task performance, initiative entropy, and satisfaction. Collaborative agents win 66-86% against autonomous ones in the real condition. Error analysis finds failures in communication, situational awareness, and personalization. No learning occurs and adaptation stays within one session, leaving cross-session, per-user interaction learning open.
papers.relation: Evaluates collaboration process, but not per-user adaptation.
papers.closest_overlap: It evaluates procedural aspects of collaboration (initiative balance, proactive confirmation, act/message/wait decisions, non-turn-taking coordination) with 99 real participants. Its error taxonomy names failure to adapt to individual in-session preferences (16% of real trajectories) and to carry preferences into future interactions (P.3). That is the gap USIL targets, but the paper results are averaged across users.
papers.remaining_question: Can the Co-Gym dual-control, non-turn-taking setup be extended with longitudinal, repeated-user sessions and per-user metrics, so that an agent could learn user-specific initiative and confirmation policies, and procedural personalization could be measured separately from task outcomes?

papers.title: Comparing Human Oversight Strategies for Computer-Use Agents
papers.authors: Chaoran Chen, Zhiping Zhang, Zeya Chen, et al.
papers.cite_role: Evidence: no single oversight strategy is best for all users
papers.summary: This paper compares four human-oversight strategies for LLM computer-use agents (Risk-Gated, Action Confirmation, Supervisory Co-Execution, Structurally Enriched) in 192 live sessions with a shared base agent and task environment. Plan-based strategies reduced the odds of problematic actions by 76%, but users blocked only 29 of 138 problematic actions that reached execution, with no reliable difference across strategies. Video coding shows that authority is often mistimed and that users check procedural correctness. The authors argue that oversight should adapt over time, but nothing is learned or personalized, and there is no transfer evaluation. It is useful as population-level evidence on procedural interaction timing.
papers.what_is_learned: other: none learned (comparison of fixed oversight/interaction designs)
papers.user_evidence: interventions/corrections during execution, exposure to risky actions, trust and subjective ratings, qualitative interviews
papers.decisions_raw: confirm, intervene, ask (plan approval vs. step-level oversight)
papers.relation: Shows that the right confirmation and intervention structure depends on context and on how recognizable risky moments are, which is what USIL's ask/act/confirm policy decides. Open question: can an agent learn per user which moments that user treats as decision-critical, instead of using one fixed oversight strategy?
papers.closest_overlap: It studies the procedural side of human-agent work: when a GUI agent should hand control back through confirmation, plan approval or risk-flagged escalation, and how users delegate, inspect and intervene. It shows that these timing choices matter for safety. This is the procedure_averaged cell that USIL contrasts with per-user policies.
papers.remaining_question: Do users differ systematically in how they delegate, inspect and intervene, and so in the right timing and granularity of control return? Could a per-user policy learned from approvals, interventions and takeovers over repeated sessions fix the mistimed authority that this paper finds under population-level strategies?

papers.title: Delegating or Doing? Understanding User Behavior in Hybrid Human-Agent Interfaces
papers.authors: Gavin Dizon, Tyrone Justin Sta Maria, Jordan Aiko Deja, Yasuyuki Sumi
papers.cite_role: Key evidence: individual differences explain ~half of delegation variance (ICC=.50)
papers.summary: This between-subjects study (N=73) compares Traditional GUI, AI-First and Hybrid modes in an LLM-augmented REST web app built with an MCP architecture, using 16 CRUD tasks. AI assistance reduced clicks, navigations and scrolling but did not change task time. In the Hybrid condition, chat use did not differ significantly by CRUD operation, yet the by-participant intercept explained about half the variance (ICC=.50), so delegation varies more across users than tasks. No model is trained and nothing is personalized; adaptive designs are only suggested. The sample is homogeneous, with a single app and model and one fixed task order, so transfer is untested.
papers.what_is_learned: other: none learned (empirical characterization of per-user delegation tendencies)
papers.user_evidence: per-user choice to delegate vs. directly manipulate, interaction logs (clicks, navigation, scrolling), task outcomes
papers.relation: Direct empirical support for USIL's premise that delegation is a property of the user more than of the task. Open question: can an agent estimate this user-level delegation tendency from a few early interactions and adjust its own initiative to match?
papers.closest_overlap: The Hybrid condition lets users choose per task between GUI manipulation and delegating to an LLM agent, and the finding that delegation varies far more across users than tasks (ICC=.50) is direct empirical motivation for treating the individual user as a unit for procedural adaptation.
papers.remaining_question: Can a per-user delegation or autonomy policy be learned from a few logged GUI-versus-chat choices (the ICC=.50 signal) and shown to beat a population-level default for when the agent should act, ask or hand control back, and does it stay stable across applications, models and sessions?

papers.title: Modeling Distinct Human Interaction in Web Agents
papers.authors: Faria Huq, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Zhanqiu Guo, Venu Arvind Arangarajan, Tianyue Ou, Frank Xu, Shuyan Zhou, Graham Neubig, Jeffrey P. Bigham
papers.cite_role: Evidence: distinct individual intervention styles with web agents
papers.summary: The paper introduces modeling human intervention in collaborative web agents. COWCORPUS holds 400 real-user trajectories (20 users, 20 tasks each) with over 4,200 interleaved human and agent actions. K-means clustering yields four interaction styles: Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off and Collaborative. Fine-tuned LMMs (Gemma-27B, LLaVA-8B) predict at each step whether the user will intervene and outperform prompted closed models on Perfect Timing Score. Style-conditioned models generally do best on their own cluster, except Takeover. In a small user study (n=16), the deployed PlowPilot, which prompts only when intervention is likely, was rated 36.8% more useful than CowPilot. Personalization is at cluster level, with no cross-session adaptation or transfer shown.
papers.relation: Close predecessor showing individual intervention styles; open question is adapting the agent's own policy to each style.
papers.closest_overlap: It is close to USIL's procedural focus: it learns when an agent should hand control to the user (ask vs. continue) from real interleaved human-agent web trajectories, and conditions the policy on interaction style (Takeover, Hands-on, Hands-off, Collaborative). The style-conditioned models are an intermediate step between averaged and individual interaction policies [personalization][what_is_learned].
papers.remaining_question: Do style-cluster models extend to per-user pi_u that adapt online from a few interventions for a new user, including the data-sparse Takeover-like users, and do they transfer to unseen tasks, sites, and users across sessions? The paper does not establish this [transfer][temporal_adaptation][limitations].

papers.title: Programming by Chat: A Large-Scale Behavioral Analysis of 11,579 Real-World AI-Assisted IDE Sessions

papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Analysis of about 75K developer messages from roughly 11.6K Cursor/Copilot chat sessions (899 developers, 1.3K repositories) committed to public repositories. Developers refine iteratively instead of specifying tasks upfront, delegate diagnosis, comprehension, and validation, and manage collaboration by saving plans as persistent artifacts and limiting agent autonomy through context injection and behavioral constraints.
papers.what_is_learned: other: none learned (observational characterization of real-world interaction patterns)
papers.user_evidence: real-world chat logs, refinements/corrections, user-written persistent plans and rules files
papers.relation: In the wild, users already encode interaction preferences by hand, as persistent plans and behavioral constraints. Open question: can an agent infer and maintain these per-user interaction rules from corrections instead of requiring users to write them?

papers.title: Autonomy Reshapes How Personalization Affects Privacy Concerns and Trust in LLM Agents
papers.authors: Zhiping Zhang, Yi Evie Zhang, Freda Shi, Tianshi Li
papers.cite_role: Alternative view: privacy and trust costs of personalization
papers.summary: A 3x3 between-subjects experiment (N=450) crosses LLM agent autonomy (none, full, risk-contingent) with personalization (none, privacy-aware, full) in message-sending scenarios using participants' real personal information. Full personalization raises privacy concern and lowers trust. Risk-contingent autonomy, where the agent hands control back to the user when a GPT-4o detector flags sensitive content, attenuates these effects, and perceived control mediates this. Full autonomy shows no significant effects. Nothing is learned: the policy is fixed, personalization is by prompting, and the study is single-session with two scenarios. It offers empirical grounding for adaptive autonomy and return-of-control design, but not per-user learning.
papers.what_is_learned: other: none learned (experimental comparison of autonomy designs)
papers.user_evidence: self-reported privacy concern, trust, perceived control, willingness to use
papers.relation: Shows that returning control at risky moments raises perceived control, and points to a tension: the personal data USIL learns from can itself erode trust. Open question: can the triggers for returning control be learned per user while keeping user-model privacy costs acceptable?
papers.closest_overlap: Its risk-contingent autonomy has the agent withhold a message and return control to the user when a GPT-4o detector flags sensitive content, and it shows this changes how personalization affects trust and privacy concern, with perceived control as the mediator [interaction_decisions] [key_results]. This is evidence that autonomy and return-of-control policy matter for user perception. However, the policy is fixed and population-level, and personalization is prompt-based.
papers.remaining_question: Can the risk threshold for handing back control be learned per user, using their own sensitivity labels, approvals, and rejections, and does that further raise perceived control and trust beyond the fixed risk-contingent policy? Does it persist over repeated sessions and other contexts?

papers.title: Towards Optimizing Human-Centric Objectives in AI-Assisted Decision-Making With Offline Reinforcement Learning
papers.authors: Zana Buçinca, Siddharth Swaroop, Amanda E. Paluch, Susan A. Murphy, Krzysztof Z. Gajos
papers.cite_role: User-conditioned assistance policy learned with offline RL
papers.summary: The paper proposes offline RL to learn AI-assistance policies in AI-assisted decision-making that optimize human-centric objectives, namely immediate accuracy and learning. A tabular Q-learning policy over a 64-state space (Need for Cognition, concept, AI correctness, knowledge) selects among four assistance types. Policies are learned from data on 142 participants making exercise-prescription decisions, then tested in two new studies. Accuracy-optimized policies beat baselines for both NFC groups, sometimes achieving complementarity. Learning-optimized policies helped only low-NFC users in Experiment 1 and showed no significant effect in Experiment 2. Personalization is group-level, with a single task and crowd participants, and no transfer is tested.
papers.what_is_learned: interaction policy (which form of assistance to give, conditioned on user and task state)
papers.user_evidence: logged decisions and outcomes under different assistance types, user traits (e.g., need for cognition), task features
papers.relation: Closest existing example of a user-conditioned assistance policy learned with RL from interaction logs. Open question: can the policy be adapted online for a single user from that user's sparse evidence, rather than conditioned on population-level traits?
papers.closest_overlap: It learns an adaptive policy over how AI assistance is delivered (explanation, recommendation, withholding) with offline RL, conditioned on a user trait (Need for Cognition) and on running knowledge, and it optimizes human-centric objectives such as learning instead of accuracy only. This is close to USIL's idea of a user-conditioned interaction policy, but conditioning is on two NFC groups, not individual histories.
papers.remaining_question: Can offline RL policies of this type be conditioned on individual interaction history (edits, overrides, reliance patterns) rather than a median-split NFC group, and still deliver gains in accuracy and learning across sessions, tasks, and expert users, given that learning gains were weak and non-replicated in Experiment 2?

papers.title: FSPO: Few-Shot Optimization of Synthetic Preferences Personalizes to Real Users
papers.authors: Anikait Singh, Sheryl Hsu, Kyle Hsu, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Tatsunori Hashimoto, Archit Sharma, Chelsea Finn
papers.cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: outcome × individual, few-shot personalization
papers.summary: FSPO reframes LLM personalization as meta-learning over users: a single Llama 3.2 3B model, fine-tuned with IPO/DPO-style objectives, conditions on a user's few labeled preference pairs to infer a personalized reward and generate tailored answers. User description rationalization (RAT) and a synthetic pipeline of over 1M preferences, designed to be diverse and self-consistent, enable transfer from synthetic personas to real users. It reaches about 82-90% winrate on synthetic users and beats the base model (68%) and an SFT model (72%) in a preliminary 50-person human study. It also improves reward prediction on PRISM. It does not address interaction decisions or temporal adaptation.
papers.relation: Strongest few-shot personalization result; remaining question is few-shot adaptation of interaction policies rather than responses.
papers.closest_overlap: FSPO treats the individual user as the unit of learning, conditioning on few-shot user-specific preference evidence (an N-bit representation, optionally an inferred description) and showing sim2real transfer to 50 real Prolific users and held-out PRISM users. This is the outcome_individual counterpart of the USIL few-shot user adaptation and latent user-representation idea z_u=g(h).
papers.remaining_question: Can the FSPO few-shot meta-learning recipe, with synthetic personas and RAT-style rationalization, be extended to infer procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, defer or return control) instead of response-content preferences? Would sim2real transfer still hold for interaction policies, and could it be evaluated longitudinally with drifting users?

papers.title: Learning to Summarize User Information for Personalized Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback
papers.authors: Hyunji Nam, Yanming Wan, Mickel Liu, Jianxun Lian, Peter Ahnn, Natasha Jaques
papers.cite_role: Representation locus: learned textual user summaries
papers.summary: PLUS (Preference Learning Using Summarization) personalizes RLHF reward models without user IDs. A PPO-trained LLM summarizer turns each user's context, such as past conversations, into a short natural-language preference summary. A reward model conditioned on that summary predicts chosen vs. rejected responses, and the two are trained jointly. PLUS beats Bradley-Terry-Luce reward models by 11–77% on Pets and UltraFeedback and stays above 90% accuracy under topic shift. On PRISM it beats baselines for in-distribution users but not held-out users. Summaries also personalize GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 without fine-tuning (72% and 69% win rates). The work addresses output preference only: it does not model temporal drift or interaction decisions such as asking or deferring.
papers.relation: Interpretable representation locus for USIL; could summaries capture procedural preferences?
papers.closest_overlap: PLUS is the closest outcome_individual counterpart to USIL. It infers a per-user latent z as an editable natural-language summary from sparse interaction history, which could serve as the z_u = g(h) component in USIL's pi_u(a|s,h^u). It uses user-specific evidence (past conversations and preferences) to personalize, but only for reward and response quality.
papers.remaining_question: Can PLUS-style text summaries encode procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer, how much autonomy to take) and condition an interaction policy rather than a reward model? Do they update as a user's preferences drift across sessions, and do they transfer to held-out users, where PLUS lost to BTL/DPL on PRISM (59.7 vs 62.9/65.3)?

papers.title: AI Alignment with Changing and Influenceable Reward Functions
papers.authors: Micah Carroll, Davis Foote, Anand Siththaranjan, Stuart Russell, Anca Dragan
papers.cite_role: Changing and influenceable preferences: limits on legitimate adaptation
papers.summary: This ICML 2024 paper introduces Dynamic Reward MDPs (DR-MDPs) to analyze AI decision-making when a person's reward function changes over time and can be influenced by the AI. It shows that common alignment objectives, such as real-time reward and initial reward, can incentivize undesirable influence, lock-in, or poor real-time reward, and that changing the horizon cannot reliably remove these incentives. Comparing 8 notions of alignment on toy examples, it finds each either permits undesirable influence or is overly risk-averse, with the proposed ParetoUD often reducing to inaction. The work is purely theoretical: reward functions and their dynamics are assumed known, with no user data or learning.
papers.relation: Key reference for preference drift and influence; USIL inherits the question of which adaptation is legitimate.
papers.closest_overlap: DR-MDPs formalize preferences that change over time and respond to the AI's own actions. This is the drift-versus-influence problem USIL faces when adapting a pi_u to evolving user evidence: an agent learning from a user's reactions can shift the user it is modeling. The analysis of real-time, initial, final and natural-shift objectives and of horizon effects speaks directly to what a longitudinal per-user policy should optimize [temporal_adaptation][key_results].

papers.authors: Ge Gao, Alexey Taymanov, Eduardo Salinas, Paul Mineiro, Dipendra Misra
papers.cite_role: Learning latent preferences from user edits
papers.summary: PRELUDE/CIPHER studies how a frozen LLM agent can learn from user edits to its outputs. The LLM infers a natural-language description of the user's latent preference from each (output, edit) pair. At test time, descriptions from the k most similar past contexts are aggregated into the prompt, so no fine-tuning is needed. In GPT-4 simulated-user summarization and email-writing environments, CIPHER cuts cumulative edit cost by 31% and 73% against baselines and has the best preference accuracy. A small human study supports this. It does not cover interaction decisions, drift, or transfer, and a gap to the oracle remains.
papers.relation: Learns from naturally occurring edits over time; affects what is produced, not when to ask or act.
papers.closest_overlap: CIPHER learns an individual user's latent, context-dependent preference from implicit feedback (edits) via retrieval over interaction history, with no fine-tuning. It is close to USIL's user-specific evidence and h_t^u memory, and an edit-triggered LPI skip (δ threshold) is the nearest thing to an adaptive interaction choice. The learned object is output style, not interaction behavior.
papers.remaining_question: Can edit-derived preference descriptions be extended to procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) and be tested with real, evolving users and cross-task transfer, rather than a GPT-4 simulated user with fixed per-source preferences?

papers.title: Personalizing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback with Variational Preference Learning
papers.authors: Sriyash Poddar, Yanming Wan, Hamish Ivison, Abhishek Gupta, Natasha Jaques
papers.cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: outcome × individual (latent user variable)
papers.summary: VPL personalizes RLHF by treating each user's preferences as a latent variable. A variational encoder infers a user latent z from a handful of that user's preference-pair annotations. A latent-conditioned BTL reward model and policies then adapt to the user without further training. The paper adds likelihood-based reward scaling (VPL-SPO) and active query selection that picks informative pairs, roughly halving the queries needed in simulated control. VPL beats BTL and DPL baselines on simulated control tasks and LLM reward modeling (e.g. 74.75 vs 49.84 on UF-P-2) and matches BTL on unimodal data. Users are simulated, preferences are static, and transfer is not evaluated. It is a strong outcome_individual predecessor.
papers.relation: Latent-variable personalization for outcomes; open question is whether the same machinery can condition interaction decisions (ask/act).
papers.closest_overlap: VPL infers a user-specific latent z from a few of the user's own preference annotations, which acts as z_u = g(h) in USIL. It conditions a reward model and policy on z at test time without retraining. Its mutual-information active querying is an explicit per-user elicitation decision, so it overlaps with P1, P2 and the asking part of P3.
papers.remaining_question: Can VPL's latent-user inference and active querying be extended from static, simulated preferences over outputs to real users' procedural preferences (when to ask, confirm, or defer) that drift across sessions? That would need real-user data and evaluation of transfer to new tasks or users.

papers.title: Position: A Roadmap to Pluralistic Alignment
papers.authors: Taylor Sorensen et al.
papers.cite_role: Sibling position paper (pluralistic alignment)
papers.summary: This ICML 2024 position paper proposes a roadmap to pluralistic alignment. It formalizes three kinds of pluralistic models: Overton (a spectrum of reasonable responses), steerable (conditioned on attributes), and distributional (matching a population distribution). It also formalizes three kinds of benchmarks: multi-objective, trade-off steerable, and jury-pluralistic. A small experiment on GlobalOpinionQA and MPI finds that most post-alignment LLMs have higher Jensen-Shannon distance to human answer distributions and lower entropy than their base models, which the authors treat as initial rather than conclusive evidence. No model is trained, no individual user data is used, and interaction decisions and temporal adaptation are not addressed. It is useful framing for USIL's outcome-side and evaluation discussion.
papers.relation: Close in genre (position paper) and in arguing against averaging; focuses on values/outputs rather than how an agent works with a user.
papers.closest_overlap: Its steerable pluralism, M(x, a) conditioned on an attribute, and its jury-pluralistic benchmark with per-juror reward models resemble a user-conditioned policy. The jury idea also resembles evaluating against individual raters instead of an average. However, the conditioning is on values, groups, or personas and concerns what the model outputs, not how the agent interacts [personalization][what_is_learned].
papers.remaining_question: Can steerable and jury-pluralistic benchmarks be extended from conditioning outputs on value attributes to measuring per-user procedural adaptation, such as when to ask, confirm, or defer, across sessions? And does the finding that alignment reduces distributional pluralism also hold for interaction behaviors, i.e. does RLHF collapse the diversity of interaction styles?

papers.title: The PRISM Alignment Dataset: What Participatory, Representative and Individualised Human Feedback Reveals About the Subjective and Multicultural Alignment of Large Language Models
papers.authors: Hannah Rose Kirk, Alexander Whitefield, Paul Röttger, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Collects multi-turn conversations and fine-grained ratings from 1,500 participants in 75 countries, linked to each person's sociodemographic profile and stated preferences, and documents substantial heterogeneity in preferences across individuals and groups.
papers.what_is_learned: other: dataset of individualized preferences linked to user profiles
papers.user_evidence: Per-user surveys (stated preferences, demographics) plus ratings and choices in live multi-turn conversations
papers.relation: One of the few datasets that links individual users to their interaction-level feedback; it covers output preferences only, so it leaves open how much users differ on interaction-policy preferences such as how often they want to be asked.

papers.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model Is Secretly a Reward Model
papers.authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Optimizes a policy directly from preference pairs without an explicit reward model.
papers.relation: Population-level objective; a common backbone for personalized variants.

papers.title: Personalized Soups: Personalized Large Language Model Alignment via Post-hoc Parameter Merging
papers.authors: Joel Jang, Seungone Kim, Bill Yuchen Lin, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Frames personalization as multi-objective RL (RLPHF): trains separate policies or reward signals per preference dimension and composes them at inference by post-hoc parameter merging, so each user's combination of preferences can be served without retraining.
papers.user_evidence: Pairwise preference feedback along declared preference dimensions (e.g., concise vs. elaborate, friendly vs. unfriendly)
papers.relation: Composing per-dimension policies is a way to represent a user's preferences; the open question is whether interaction-policy dimensions (ask vs. act, confirm thresholds) can be merged the same way and inferred from behavior rather than declared.

papers.title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback
papers.authors: Long Ouyang et al.
papers.cite_role: 2x2 exemplar: outcome × averaged (standard RLHF)
papers.summary: InstructGPT fine-tunes GPT-3 in three steps: supervised learning on labeler demonstrations, a reward model trained on labeler rankings, and PPO against that reward model, with a pretraining-mix variant (PPO-ptx) to reduce regressions. Labelers prefer the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3. Truthfulness improves and toxicity falls when the model is prompted to be respectful, but bias does not improve. Alignment is to an aggregate of about 40 contracted labelers and researchers, not to individual users. The model is single-turn, learns no interaction policy, and does not adapt over time. The authors discuss group-conditioned preferences only as future work. It is useful as the outcome-averaged baseline for USIL.
papers.relation: Canonical averaged-outcome alignment (the averaged/outcome cell of the 2x2).
papers.closest_overlap: InstructGPT is the canonical outcome_averaged baseline for USIL. Its labelers' demonstrations, rankings and pairwise comparisons are the same kinds of user evidence USIL uses, but pooled into one reward model. The Discussion section acknowledges that one cannot align to everyone at once and proposes group-conditioned models as future work [personalization].
papers.remaining_question: Could the same SFT/RM/PPO pipeline learn per-user reward models or interaction policies, for example when to ask, confirm, or refuse, from a few of one user's own edits and approvals, given that labelers here are not the users who wrote the prompts [user_evidence]? How would that be evaluated beyond averaged labeler win rates?

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning from Human Preferences
papers.authors: Paul F. Christiano, Jan Leike, Tom B. Brown, Miljan Martic, Shane Legg, Dario Amodei
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Learns a reward model from pairwise human preference comparisons to train RL agents without hand-specified rewards.
papers.relation: Foundation of preference learning; aggregates across labelers, so the per-user and procedural dimensions USIL targets are absent.

papers.title: Ask Early, Ask Late, Ask Right: When Does Clarification Timing Matter for Long-Horizon Agents?
papers.authors: Anmol Gulati, Hariom Gupta, Elias Lumer, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Injects ground-truth clarifications at controlled points in long-horizon agent trajectories across four information types (goal, input, constraint, context), finding that value depends strongly on timing and type (goal clarification nearly worthless after ~10% of execution; late clarification can be worse than none) and that current models over-ask or never ask.
papers.what_is_learned: other: empirical characterization of clarification value vs. timing
papers.user_evidence: Injected ground-truth clarifications; 300 unscripted agent sessions
papers.relation: Adds the timing dimension to when-to-ask in agentic workflows; open question is whether optimal timing also varies by user (e.g., users who prefer upfront specification vs. mid-task check-ins) and can be learned.

papers.title: Value of Information: A Framework for Human–Agent Communication
papers.authors: Yijiang River Dong, Tiancheng Hu, Zheng Hui, Caiqi Zhang, Ivan Vulić, Andreea Bobu, Nigel Collier
papers.cite_role: Value-of-information rule for when to ask (population costs)
papers.summary: The paper proposes a decision-theoretic, inference-time Value of Information framework for LLM agents deciding whether to ask a clarifying question or act on an underspecified request. The LLM estimates a belief over latent user intent, simulates the answers to candidate questions, and asks only when expected utility gain exceeds the communication cost. It needs no threshold tuning. Across 20 Questions, flight preference, and ambiguous WebShop, with GPT-4.1 and Gemini-2.5-Flash, VoI matches or beats tuned baselines in 18 of 20 conditions, but trails at higher costs. Users are simulated, and adaptation is limited to a single dialogue. It is a strong population-level procedural baseline for USIL.
papers.relation: Principled when-to-ask rule with population-level costs; per-user costs are the USIL gap.
papers.closest_overlap: The VoI clarify-or-commit policy is a principled, tuning-free instantiation of the ask-versus-act decision (P3) that USIL wants to make user-specific. The flight-preference task infers a latent per-user reward function from five rounds of choice history plus clarifying questions [personalization], so it does touch on per-user inference within a dialogue.
papers.remaining_question: Can the VoI communication cost c and the stakes or utility scale be learned per user, for example from interruptions, answer latency or skipped questions, so the ask/commit threshold becomes user-specific and persists across sessions with real users rather than simulated ones?

papers.title: When Users Change Their Mind: Evaluating Interruptible Agents in Long-Horizon Web Navigation
papers.authors: Henry Peng Zou, Chunyu Miao, Wei-Chieh Huang, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Introduces InterruptBench (from WebArena-Lite) with three interruption types (addition, revision, retraction) mid-execution, evaluating how well six LLM agents adapt to updated goals and recover efficiently; finds interruption handling remains hard for strong models.
papers.what_is_learned: other: benchmark of agent adaptation to user interruptions
papers.user_evidence: Mid-task user interruptions (goal additions, revisions, retractions)
papers.relation: Treats interruptions as a feedback type agents must handle within a task; open question is whether interruption patterns can be learned as user evidence to anticipate a user's changes or to confirm earlier.

papers.title: CollabLLM: From Passive Responders to Active Collaborators
papers.authors: Shirley Wu, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
papers.cite_role: Learning when to ask/suggest, but for a population
papers.summary: CollabLLM trains LLMs to be active collaborators in multiturn dialogue. It estimates Multiturn-aware Rewards by simulating future turns with an LLM user simulator, then fine-tunes Llama-3.1-8B with SFT, DPO, or PPO. The resulting policy asks clarifying questions and makes suggestions when requests are ambiguous. In simulation it improves task performance by 18.5%, interactivity by 46.3%, and efficiency by 13.3%. A 201-person user study shows 17.6% higher satisfaction and 10.4% less time spent. Zero-shot transfer to Abg-CoQA shows more clarification. It does no per-user personalization or cross-session adaptation, and the authors list personalization as future work.
papers.user_evidence: Simulated user responses over future turns (rollouts) scored for task success, efficiency and engagement; no real per-user data in training
papers.decisions_raw: ask, clarify, suggest (proactive intervention) vs. answer
papers.relation: Learns a population-level when-to-ask/suggest policy via long-horizon reward; open question is whether the multiturn-aware reward can be conditioned on an individual user's history so that clarification frequency adapts per user.
papers.closest_overlap: CollabLLM learns an interaction policy for when to ask clarifying questions, offer suggestions, or answer directly, by optimizing multiturn-aware rewards with simulated users. It is a population-level (procedure_averaged) version of what USIL wants per user, and it shows that forward-looking RL can shift asking behavior (~50% clarification on ambiguous inputs zero-shot) [interaction_decisions][transfer].
papers.remaining_question: Can Multiturn-aware Rewards be conditioned on a user-specific history h_u, with simulators that vary in how often they want to be asked or how much autonomy they grant, so that the clarify/suggest/act policy adapts per user over sessions and not just within a conversation? Does that still hold when real users differ from the simulators?

papers.title: Eliciting Human Preferences with Language Models
papers.authors: Belinda Z. Li, Alex Tamkin, Noah Goodman, Jacob Andreas
papers.cite_role: Representative active preference-elicitation method; contrast what to ask with learning when to ask
papers.summary: The paper introduces Generative Active Task Elicitation (GATE). Instead of users writing prompts or labeling examples, a language model interviews them with open-ended questions, yes/no questions or generated edge cases for five minutes. A GPT-4 predictor conditioned on the transcript then predicts that user's labels. Across content recommendation, moral reasoning and email validation, GATE often beats user-written prompts, supervised learning and pool-based active learning, with equal or lower reported mental effort. No model is trained, the question policy is prompt-only, and adaptation is single-session. It is a close predecessor for per-user elicitation but targets output preferences, not interaction procedure.
papers.relation: Active elicitation per user; question budget and per-user cost of asking are open.
papers.closest_overlap: GATE elicits each user's preferences with LM-generated open-ended questions and edge cases, then conditions a predictor on that user's transcript and scores per-user agreement. This is per-user adaptation from user answers, the same evidence type USIL names. The policy chooses which question to ask, which overlaps with USIL's ask/clarify decisions.
papers.remaining_question: GATE elicits preferences about the task output (what content to recommend, moral judgments, email validity). Can the same elicitation learn how a user wants the agent to behave (when to ask, confirm or defer), and do those elicited interaction preferences persist and transfer across sessions and tasks? The questioning policy is also the same for every user. Could it be adapted per user?

papers.title: Learning to Clarify: Multi-turn Conversations with Action-Based Contrastive Self-Training
papers.authors: Maximillian Chen, Ruoxi Sun, Tomas Pfister, Sercan Ö. Arık
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Proposes ACT, a quasi-online DPO variant that contrasts dialogue actions (clarify vs. answer) using on-policy multi-turn rollouts with a user simulator, learning data-efficient clarification policies; introduces AmbigSQL and evaluates on tabular QA and reading comprehension.
papers.user_evidence: Small sets of conversations with implicit action labels plus simulated user replies during self-training
papers.relation: Shows that action-level preference learning can shape ask-vs-act from little data, a natural mechanism for few-shot user adaptation; untested whether per-user action preferences (from approvals/rejections) can be learned the same way.

papers.title: Modeling Future Conversation Turns to Teach LLMs to Ask Clarifying Questions
papers.authors: Michael J. Q. Zhang, W. Bradley Knox, Eunsol Choi
papers.cite_role: Representative clarification-policy method; include if needed to distinguish when versus what to ask
papers.summary: The paper teaches LLMs (Llama2, Gemma, Llama3) to ask clarifying questions for ambiguous QA by labeling DPO preferences through simulated future turns. A user simulator answers the clarifying question, and the downstream answer's F1 against each interpretation's gold answer decides whether asking or answering directly is preferred. This double-turn labeling gives about 5% higher F1 than single-turn preferences. A clarify-or-direct model also learns when clarification is needed and beats a random baseline. Users are simulated from dataset annotations, interactions last at most two turns, and there is no cross-session or per-user adaptation. Transfer to other tasks is left as future work.
papers.user_evidence: Annotated/simulated user answers to clarifying questions and resulting final-answer quality across multiple annotated interpretations
papers.relation: Directly tackles when-to-ask via future-turn credit assignment; remaining question is how to make the ask/answer threshold user-specific (some users prefer guesses, others prefer questions) from sparse feedback.
papers.closest_overlap: It trains an LLM policy over ask-versus-answer decisions, using simulated users to score the future consequences of asking. This is the population-level clarification policy that USIL treats as the procedure_averaged baseline. Preference labels are kept per simulated annotator/interpretation, which loosely resembles user-conditioned evidence, but only within one conversation.
papers.remaining_question: Could the double-turn simulated-outcome preference labeling be conditioned on a persistent user history, so that the clarify-versus-answer threshold adapts to an individual user's tolerance for questions and ambiguity-resolution habits, rather than being a single population policy trained against simulated gold-answer users?

papers.title: Structured Uncertainty guided Clarification for LLM Agents
papers.authors: Manan Suri, Puneet Mathur, Nedim Lipka, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Models uncertainty over tool parameters and values and scores candidate clarifying questions by Expected Value of Perfect Information with a redundancy cost (SAGE-Agent), asking fewer questions with better coverage; uses the uncertainty as an RL (GRPO) signal and introduces ClarifyBench for multi-turn tool-calling disambiguation.
papers.user_evidence: Simulated user answers to clarifying questions about tool arguments
papers.decisions_raw: ask/clarify vs. act (tool call), when to stop asking
papers.relation: Operationalizes value-of-information for agent clarification with an explicit question cost; open question is learning a user-specific question cost and prior over parameter values from that user's past answers.

papers.title: Bayesian Preference Elicitation with Language Models
papers.authors: Kunal Handa, Yarin Gal, Ellie Pavlick, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Proposes OPEN, combining Bayesian optimal experimental design (to choose the most informative query over LM-extracted features) with an LM that verbalizes queries in natural language; user studies show better preference elicitation than LM-only or BOED-only baselines.
papers.user_evidence: User answers to natural-language preference questions
papers.relation: Principled information-gain question selection with an explicit per-user posterior; open question is extending the posterior to interaction preferences (not just item preferences) and deciding when the information is worth the user's effort.

papers.title: Introspective Planning: Aligning Robots' Uncertainty with Inherent Task Ambiguity
papers.authors: Kaiqu Liang, Zixu Zhang, Jaime Fernández Fisac
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Robots introspect over uncertainty to decide when to ask for clarification, with conformal guarantees.
papers.relation: Calibrated asking under ambiguity; thresholds are not user-specific.

papers.title: STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
papers.authors: Chinmaya Andukuri, Jan-Philipp Fränken, Tobias Gerstenberg, Noah D. Goodman
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Self-improvement loop that trains LMs to ask useful clarifying questions with simulated users.
papers.relation: Learns to ask well, but for a population of simulated users.

papers.title: Tell Me More! Towards Implicit User Intention Understanding of Language Model Driven Agents
papers.authors: Cheng Qian, Bingxiang He, Zhong Zhuang, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Introduces the Intention-in-Interaction (IN3) benchmark for detecting vague agent tasks and eliciting implicit user intentions through explicit questions, and trains Mistral-Interact as an upstream module that judges vagueness, queries missing details, and summarizes intent into goals before XAgent executes.
papers.user_evidence: User answers to clarifying questions about missing task details (simulated and human)
papers.decisions_raw: clarify/ask vs. act; summarize intent before execution
papers.relation: Agent-level intent clarification before execution, elicited per task; open question is whether intentions elicited from a user can be stored and reused so future tasks need fewer questions.

papers.title: Robots That Ask for Help: Uncertainty Alignment for Large Language Model Planners
papers.authors: Allen Z. Ren et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: KnowNo: conformal prediction lets LLM planners ask for help when uncertain with statistical guarantees.
papers.relation: Population-level help-seeking; USIL asks how coverage levels should vary by user.

papers.title: A preference elicitation framework for automated planning
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first
papers.summary: Low-burden preference queries transfer to larger plans
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

papers.title: Unified Learning from Demonstrations, Corrections, and Preferences during Physical Human-Robot Interaction
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first
papers.summary: Integrates heterogeneous forms of robot teaching feedback
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

papers.title: Active Preference-Based Learning of Reward Functions
papers.authors: Dorsa Sadigh, Anca D. Dragan, S. Shankar Sastry, Sanjit A. Seshia
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Actively selects comparison queries to learn a human's reward function efficiently.
papers.relation: Query-efficient per-person learning; outcome rewards rather than interaction preferences.

papers.title: KnowU-Bench: Towards Interactive, Proactive, and Personalized Mobile Agent Evaluation
papers.authors: Tongbo Chen, Zhengxi Lu, Zhan Xu, et al.
papers.cite_role: Evaluation: per-user consent, intervention and restraint
papers.summary: KnowU-Bench is an online Android-emulator benchmark for interactive, proactive, and personalized mobile agents, with 42 general, 86 personalized, and 64 proactive tasks. A hidden-profile LLM user simulator (gpt-4o) supplies clarification answers and consent or rejection. Agents see only timestamped behavior logs, clean or noisy, and must infer preferences or ask. In proactive tasks they choose between acting, proposing, and staying silent, and must stop after rejection. Hybrid rule and LLM-judge scoring is used. Of 11 models, Claude Sonnet 4.6 is best (60.4% SR), but hard personalized tasks peak at 44.2%. Failures are mostly poor clarification and miscalibrated intervention. No learning or temporal adaptation is studied.
papers.what_is_learned: other: benchmark (evaluates inferred user model and intervention behavior)
papers.user_evidence: behavioral logs, answers to clarification questions, consent and rejection responses
papers.decisions_raw: ask, clarify, intervene, confirm (consent), defer (restraint after rejection)
papers.relation: Directly evaluates per-user ask/intervene/consent decisions from inferred preferences, which makes it a candidate P4 testbed; it remains open whether agents improve these decisions over repeated sessions with the same user.
papers.closest_overlap: It evaluates procedural, user-specific behavior (asking via ask_user, proposing for confirmation, staying silent, stopping after rejection) against hidden per-role profiles in a live Android environment. This is the closest benchmark to USIL's procedure-by-individual cell [interaction_decisions][personalization].
papers.remaining_question: KnowU-Bench uses four synthetic personas with static logs and no learning. Can agents learn a per-user interaction policy (when to ask, act, or stay silent) from accumulating corrections and rejections over sessions, and does it transfer to new tasks and apps? The benchmark does not test this [temporal_adaptation][transfer].

table1.name: KnowU-Bench
table1.learns: Benchmark: act, ask, or stay silent

papers.title: Latent Preference Modeling for Multi-Session Personalized Tool Calling
papers.authors: Yejin Yoon, Minseo Kim, Taeuk Kim
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Introduces MPT, a benchmark of 4,695 instances from 459 multi-session histories that tests preference recall, inference and transfer when users leave out tool arguments, and PRefine, a test-time memory that keeps a textual hypothesis of latent user preferences and refines it with a generate-verify-refine loop; PRefine beats existing memory systems and full-history prompting on transfer.
papers.user_evidence: multi-session interaction history (past tool calls and choices)
papers.decisions_raw: act (filling under-specified tool arguments by inference instead of asking)
papers.relation: Shows that distilling history into preference hypotheses transfers better than raw memory, which is an argument for P2-style representations; it covers what to infer but not when inference is uncertain enough that the agent should ask instead.

papers.title: Learning Next Action Predictors from Human-Computer Interaction
papers.authors: Omar Shaikh et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Trains models to predict a user's next action from interaction traces.
papers.relation: Predicting what a user will do differs from learning how the user wants the agent to behave.

papers.title: Toward Personalized LLM-Powered Agents: Foundations, Evaluation, and Future Directions
papers.authors: Yue Xu, Qian Chen, Zizhan Ma, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: A survey that organizes work on personalized LLM agents around four capabilities (profile modeling, memory, planning, action execution), analyzes how user signals move through the agent pipeline, and reviews metrics, benchmarks and applications.
papers.relation: The most current map of personalized-agent work, useful for positioning; its taxonomy centers on profile, memory, planning and action content, and has no dedicated slot for personalizing the interaction policy (ask/act/defer).

papers.title: User Preference Modeling for Conversational LLM Agents: Weak Rewards from Retrieval-Augmented Interaction
papers.authors: Yuren Hao, Shuhaib Mehri, ChengXiang Zhai, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Proposes VARS, a frozen-backbone method that keeps a long-term and a short-term vector per user in a shared preference space, uses them to steer retrieval from structured preference memory, and updates them online from weak scalar feedback; on MultiSessionCollab it matches a strong reflection baseline on task success while reducing timeouts and user effort.
papers.user_evidence: weak scalar feedback from multi-session interactions (simulated users)
papers.decisions_raw: none directly (reduces user effort and timeouts; no explicit ask/act policy)
papers.relation: Online per-user latent vectors updated from sparse feedback across sessions closely match USIL P1/P2; the open question is whether such vectors can condition interaction decisions (ask vs. act) rather than only memory retrieval.

papers.title: Creating General User Models from Computer Use
papers.authors: Omar Shaikh, Shardul Sapkota, Shan Rizvi, Eric Horvitz, Joon Sung Park, Diyi Yang, Michael S. Bernstein
papers.cite_role: Persistent general user models from computer use
papers.summary: The paper presents General User Models (GUMs): per-user collections of natural-language, confidence-weighted propositions learned from unstructured computer observations (screenshots, notifications, emails) by prompting off-the-shelf LLMs and VLMs. A Propose, Retrieve, Revise, Audit pipeline updates propositions over time with decay scores. Applications query the GUM, including Gumbo, a proactive assistant that uses an expected-utility rule and rate limiting to decide when to interrupt. An email study (N=18) shows retrieval and revision improve win rate and calibration; a five-day Gumbo deployment (N=5) gives 0.79 accuracy, though only 25% of suggestions were rated strong or excellent. Cross-application transfer is claimed but not systematically tested.
papers.relation: Rich persistent user model; how such a model should drive ask/act decisions is open.
papers.closest_overlap: Each user builds their own GUM from interaction evidence, which persists and is revised over time, and Gumbo's expected-utility interruption rule with feedback fed back into the GUM touches on per-user autonomy and interruption decisions [personalization][interaction_decisions][temporal_adaptation]. This is close to USIL's z_u = g(h) and pi_u idea, but the GUM mainly models what the user knows, believes and prefers (outcome-individual) and does not learn an interaction policy.
papers.remaining_question: Can GUM-style propositions be extended to capture procedural preferences (when this user wants to be asked, interrupted, or confirmed, or to take over), with the interruption utility and thresholds learned per user from thumbs and text feedback and tested across tasks and users, rather than set from elicited costs and a fixed 1-per-minute limit?

papers.title: Know Me, Respond to Me: Benchmarking LLMs for Dynamic User Profiling and Personalized Responses at Scale
papers.authors: Bowen Jiang, Zhuoqun Hao, Young-Min Cho, et al. (incl. Lyle Ungar, Camillo J. Taylor, Dan Roth)
papers.cite_role: Evaluation template for preference drift (content, not interaction)
papers.summary: PERSONAMEM is a benchmark of 20 synthetic personas with over 180 multi-session user-chatbot histories (up to 1M tokens), generated with GPT-4o. Seven in-situ query types test recalling facts, tracking evolving preferences, and generalizing to new scenarios. Models choose among four candidate responses. Fifteen LLMs reach only about 50% accuracy, struggle to incorporate the user's latest state, and do poorly on new scenarios. Reasoning models show no clear advantage. RAG and Mem0 improve accuracy, with RAG usually better. The benchmark is individual-level and longitudinal, but it covers output personalization only and has no interaction decisions such as asking or deferring.
papers.user_evidence: long multi-session conversation histories with preference changes over time
papers.relation: Provides an evaluation design for preference drift across sessions (P1), but only for response content; an analogous benchmark for drifting interaction preferences, such as a growing tolerance for autonomy, does not exist.
papers.closest_overlap: PERSONAMEM evaluates individual-level personalization over long, evolving multi-session histories, including a 'generalize to new scenarios' query type and memory modules (RAG, Mem0). This matches USIL's P2 and P4 on user-specific history and cross-context transfer. It is an outcome-focused counterpart: it measures whether responses reflect the user's current profile, not how the agent works.
papers.remaining_question: Can PERSONAMEM-style persona histories and timestamped preference drift be extended with procedural signals (corrections, approvals, takeovers, ask/confirm preferences) so benchmarks can measure whether an agent learns per-user decisions about when to ask, act, or defer, beyond selecting profile-consistent responses?

papers.title: Large Language Models Empowered Personalized Web Agents
papers.authors: Hongru Cai, Yongqi Li, Wenjie Wang, Fengbin Zhu, Xiaoyu Shen, Wenjie Li, Tat-Seng Chua
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Formulates LLM-empowered personalized web agents, releases the PersonalWAB benchmark (three personalized web tasks, single-turn and multi-turn evaluation with simulated users built from user profiles and behavior histories), and proposes PUMA, which retrieves relevant past behaviors from a memory bank and aligns the agent through SFT and DPO.
papers.user_evidence: user profile, historical web behaviors (e.g., purchases, reviews)
papers.decisions_raw: act (personalized function calls and parameters); none for ask/confirm
papers.relation: A standard benchmark for personalizing what a web agent does from user history, but personalization targets action content rather than the interaction policy (when to ask or confirm).

papers.title: PersonaAgent: Bridging Memory and Action for Personalized LLM Agents
papers.authors: Weizhi Zhang, Xinyang Zhang, Chenwei Zhang, et al.
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Multi-Turn Interactions in LLMs (as 'PersonaAgent: When Large Language Model Agents Meet Personalization at Test Time'); arXiv preprint arXiv:2506.06254
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Presents a personalized agent framework with episodic and semantic memory and a personalized action (tool) module, linked by a per-user persona prompt that is refined at test time by simulating the user's recent interactions and applying textual-loss feedback.
papers.what_is_learned: other: per-user persona prompt (textual user model) plus memory
papers.user_evidence: user interaction history (recent interactions replayed at test time)
papers.decisions_raw: act (tool choice and use); none for ask/confirm
papers.relation: Test-time optimization of a textual per-user persona prompt is a candidate representation for pi_u, but it is evaluated on output and action personalization rather than on interaction decisions.

papers.title: Personalization of Large Language Models: A Survey
papers.authors: Zhehao Zhang et al.

papers.title: Robust AI Personalization Will Require a Human Context Protocol
papers.authors: Anand Shah, Tobin South, Talfan Evans, Hannah Rose Kirk, Andrew Trask, E. Glen Weyl, Michiel A. Bakker
papers.cite_role: Alternative view: portable stated preferences instead of learning
papers.summary: Position: personalization should rest on a user-owned, portable, natural-language preference layer shared across AI services.
papers.relation: Portable user context is a representation locus for USIL; open question is whether stated preferences suffice for interaction decisions.

papers.title: TidyBot: Personalized Robot Assistance with Large Language Models
papers.authors: Jimmy Wu, Rika Antonova, Adam Kan, et al. (incl. Shuran Song, Jeannette Bohg, Thomas Funkhouser)
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: A household robot infers a user's general object-placement rules by having an LLM summarize a few example placements, and these rules generalize to unseen objects (91.2% on the benchmark, 85% of objects put away in real-world tests).
papers.user_evidence: a few demonstrations or examples of the user's preferred object placements
papers.relation: Canonical example of few-shot preference summarization that generalizes to new instances; USIL would apply the same summarize-and-generalize idea to procedural and interaction preferences instead of task outcomes.

papers.title: User profiling and behavioral adaptation for HRI: A survey
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first

papers.title: User–interface agent interaction: personalization issues
papers.authors: Silvia Schiaffino, Analía Amandi
papers.cite_role: Early per-user interaction profile: warn/suggest/act, interruption timing
papers.summary: This 2004 IJHCS paper reports a questionnaire survey of 42 users with varying expertise on interface agents, using the authors' agents or MS Office assistants. It examines which user–agent interaction issues need personalization in mixed-initiative settings: assistant type, allowed assistance actions, interruptions, error tolerance, feedback and autonomy. Preferences are heterogeneous. Only 12% want a collaborative agent, 49% allow suggestions but not autonomous action, and tolerance for errors and willingness to give feedback decline over time. The authors derive eight lessons and propose a user interaction profile of situation–action pairs with probabilities. No system is built, learned or evaluated; the profiling algorithms are future work.
papers.user_evidence: observed user reactions and explicit feedback
papers.relation: Earliest direct predecessor of USIL's interaction-policy framing; pre-LLM and rule/learning-based—how does it scale to tool-using LLM agents?
papers.closest_overlap: The paper argues that mixed-initiative interaction issues (assistant type, allowed autonomy, interruption tolerance, error tolerance, feedback willingness) vary across users and need per-user profiles. It proposes a profile of situation–agent-action pairs with probabilities [what_is_learned][personalization]. This is an early, motivational form of USIL's pi_u, aimed at procedural rather than outcome personalization.
papers.remaining_question: Can per-user interaction profiles of situation–action probabilities, with confidence thresholds for autonomy and interruption, be learned from sparse behavioural traces (accept/reject, takeover, ignored suggestions) rather than self-reports? Would they track the drift in error tolerance and feedback willingness seen over time, and outperform population-level or expertise-group defaults?

papers.authors: Vishakh Padmakumar, Lujain Ibrahim, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jennifer Wang, Q. Vera Liao, Diyi Yang
