papers.title: Personalized Benchmarking: Evaluating LLMs by Individual Preferences
papers.authors: Cristina Garbacea, Heran Wang, Chenhao Tan
papers.cite_role: Evidence: individual model rankings diverge from aggregate rankings
papers.summary: The paper introduces personalized benchmarking for LLMs. Using Chatbot Arena votes from 115 users with at least 25 battles, it computes per-user ELO and Bradley-Terry rankings over 20 models and finds that they diverge from global rankings (mean Spearman 0.432 for ELO, 0.043 for BT). Users also differ in query topics and writing style. A regression on topic and style features predicts user-specific rankings better than a mean-predictor baseline that mimics an aggregate benchmark (MAE reduced by 35% for ELO and 12% for BT). It studies no interaction decisions, temporal adaptation or transfer, and the validation set is small (18 users). It is correlational.
papers.relation: Evidence that averaged evaluation misrepresents individuals—extends naturally to interaction behavior.
papers.closest_overlap: It treats the individual user as the unit of evaluation rather than the average user, showing that per-user Chatbot Arena rankings diverge from global ones (BT mean Spearman 0.043) and that topic+style features predict them better than a mean-predictor baseline. This supports USIL's critique of averaged evaluation, but only on the outcome side.
papers.remaining_question: Can individual-level divergence be shown for procedural preferences (when users want clarification, confirmation or autonomy) rather than which LLM's response they prefer? Can per-user profiles predict such preferences for new users, over time and across tasks, beyond an 18-user held-out split of the same dataset?

papers.title: PrefIx: Understand and Adapt to User Preference in Human-Agent Interaction
papers.authors: Jialin Li, Zhenhao Chen, Hanjun Luo, Hanan Salam
papers.cite_role: Closest predecessor: interaction-preference benchmark and adaptation (PrefIx)
papers.summary: PrefIx is a configurable simulation environment for evaluating how LLM agents interact, not just what they accomplish. Its Interaction-as-a-Tool paradigm casts interaction behaviors (confirmation, narration, clarification, error handling) as structured tool calls. A taxonomy of 14 preference attributes (31 settings) drives a preference-guided user simulator that expresses preferences only implicitly. Seven UX dimensions and preference alignment are scored by a validated multi-LLM-judge ensemble. Prompting four LLMs to infer preferences from a sample history improved UX by 7.6% and alignment by 18.5% on average, while generally preserving tool accuracy. Nothing is trained, and long-term adaptation, transfer and real users are not tested.
papers.relation: One of the closest predecessors (interaction preferences); check whether adaptation is longitudinal.
papers.closest_overlap: PrefIx treats procedural interaction preferences (confirmation, transparency, pacing, error handling) as the thing to infer and adapt to. It evaluates this through interaction tool calls that map onto USIL's ask/confirm/explain/defer decisions, with a P vs No_P comparison and preference-alignment scoring against ground-truth trajectories [personalization][interaction_decisions][key_results]. It is the closest benchmark-level instantiation of the procedure_individual cell.
papers.remaining_question: PrefIx uses simulated users with single, fixed preference labels and a provided history. Can agents infer and update interaction preferences online from real, sparse, evolving evidence (edits, takeovers, corrections) with compound or conflicting preferences, and carry them across sessions and tasks? Long-term adaptation and transfer are untested [temporal_adaptation][transfer][limitations].

papers.title: RealWebAssist: A Benchmark for Long-Horizon Web Assistance with Real-World Users
papers.authors: Suyu Ye, Haojun Shi, Darren Shih, Hyokun Yun, Tanya Roosta, Tianmin Shu
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Benchmark of sequences of real users' instructions to a web assistant over extended multi-website interactions, requiring agents to infer intent, track changing mental state, learn user-specific routines, and ground instructions; state-of-the-art models struggle.
papers.what_is_learned: other: none (evaluation of in-context inference of user intent and routines)
papers.user_evidence: Real users' sequential, often ambiguous spoken/typed instructions and their evolving goals within a long session
papers.decisions_raw: act (grounding); implicit inference vs. need for clarification
papers.relation: Uses real users and requires learning personal routines over a long horizon; open question is evaluating whether agents use that accumulated evidence to change how they interact (ask less, act more) rather than just what they click.

papers.title: Do LLMs Recognize Your Preferences? Evaluating Personalized Preference Following in LLMs
papers.authors: Siyan Zhao et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: PrefEval benchmark for following stated user preferences across long conversations.
papers.relation: Output-preference following; interaction decisions not evaluated.

papers.title: PersonaLens: A Benchmark for Personalization Evaluation in Conversational AI Assistants
papers.authors: Zheng Zhao, Clara Vania, Subhradeep Kayal, Naila Khan, Shay B. Cohen, Emine Yilmaz
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Builds a benchmark for personalization in task-oriented assistants using diverse user profiles with preferences and interaction histories, an LLM user agent that conducts realistic task dialogues, and an LLM judge that scores personalization, response quality, and task success.
papers.user_evidence: User profiles with detailed preferences plus past interaction histories
papers.decisions_raw: none directly (personalization judged on dialogue content)
papers.relation: Combines user simulation with per-user profiles and separates personalization from task success; open question is adding judges for interaction-policy fit (did the assistant ask/confirm as this user prefers).

papers.title: PersonalLLM: Tailoring LLMs to Individual Preferences
papers.authors: Thomas P. Zollo et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Benchmark with simulated heterogeneous users for personalization algorithms.
papers.relation: Heterogeneous-user benchmark for outputs; template for an interaction-policy analogue.

papers.title: SimulatorArena: Are User Simulators Reliable Proxies for Multi-Turn Evaluation of AI Assistants?
papers.authors: Yao Dou, Michel Galley, Baolin Peng, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Collects 909 annotated human-LLM conversations (math tutoring, document creation) to test whether LLM user simulators reproduce human messages and human ratings; profile-conditioned simulators (background, communication style) reach Spearman rho about 0.7 with human judgments, and are used to benchmark 18 assistants.
papers.what_is_learned: other: user simulator fidelity (no learning of the assistant)
papers.user_evidence: Real human conversations and ratings; user profiles for conditioning simulators
papers.relation: Directly addresses the validity of simulator-based evaluation that USIL benchmarks rely on; open question is whether profile-conditioned simulators also reproduce user-specific interaction behaviors (interruptions, corrections, takeovers), not just message style and ratings.

papers.title: UserBench: An Interactive Gym Environment for User-Centric Agents
papers.authors: Cheng Qian, Zuxin Liu, Akshara Prabhakar, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Gym environment in which simulated users start with vague goals and reveal preferences incrementally and implicitly, so tool-using agents must ask clarifying questions; finds that answers fully satisfy user intent only ~20% of the time and top models elicit under 30% of preferences.
papers.what_is_learned: other: none (evaluation/RL environment for preference elicitation)
papers.user_evidence: Simulated user replies to clarifying questions; implicit preference cues
papers.relation: Separates task completion from preference alignment and measures elicitation, but each episode is a fresh user; open question is whether agents can learn across episodes which users need to be asked and which can be inferred.

papers.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
papers.authors: Shunyu Yao, Noah Shinn, Pedram Razavi, Karthik Narasimhan
papers.cite_role: Task-success evaluation with users in the loop (contrast case)
papers.summary: τ-bench is a benchmark for tool-agent-user interaction in retail and airline domains. An LM simulates a human user with a task instruction, the agent has domain APIs and a policy document, and success is judged by comparing the final database state with an annotated goal state. The paper introduces pass^k, the probability that all k i.i.d. trials succeed, to measure reliability. Twelve LMs are tested with function calling, ReAct and Act. The best, gpt-4o, reaches 61.2% pass^1 in retail and 35.2% in airline, with pass^8 below 25% in retail. Nothing is learned and there is no personalization or longitudinal adaptation, but it is a useful procedural evaluation baseline.
papers.relation: Task-success evaluation with users in the loop, but no per-user adaptation.
papers.closest_overlap: The benchmark scores procedural interaction behavior (each turn the agent chooses between a tool call and a user message, gathers information, confirms before writes, refuses prohibited requests, and transfers to a human). It runs these with LM-simulated users with different identities and preferences [interaction_decisions][user_evidence]. This covers the procedure row and offers a simulator and reliability metric that USIL evaluation could build on.
papers.remaining_question: Can τ-bench's simulated users be extended to have persistent, individually varying interaction preferences (e.g., how often they want confirmation, how much autonomy to grant) across repeated sessions, so that per-user adaptation of ask/confirm/act behavior can be measured, with pass^k used to separate real adaptation from noise?

papers.title: LaMP: When Large Language Models Meet Personalization
papers.authors: Alireza Salemi, Sheshera Mysore, Michael Bendersky, Hamed Zamani
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Introduces LaMP, a seven-task benchmark (3 classification, 4 generation) where each example is tied to a user profile, and evaluates retrieval-augmented personalization that pulls items from the user's history into the prompt.
papers.user_evidence: User profile of past authored items (documents, ratings, tweets, emails, titles)
papers.relation: Canonical per-user benchmark, but it scores personalized outputs only; it leaves open how to benchmark user-specific interaction decisions (ask/act/confirm) conditioned on the same kind of history.

papers.title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
papers.authors: Shuyan Zhou et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Realistic web environment benchmark for autonomous agents.
papers.relation: Canonical task-success benchmark (contrast case).

papers.title: Appropriate Reliance on AI Advice: Conceptualization and the Effect of Explanations
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first
papers.summary: Appropriate reliance definition and human-centered evaluation
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P4; capabilities require full-text verification.

papers.title: Learning Personalized Agents from Human Feedback
papers.authors: Kaiqu Liang, Julia Kruk, Shengyi Qian, Xianjun Yang, Shengjie Bi, Yuanshun Yao, Shaoliang Nie, Mingyang Zhang, Lijuan Liu, Jaime Fernández Fisac, Shuyan Zhou, Saghar Hosseini
papers.cite_role: Closest predecessor: clarification + per-user memory + feedback (PAHF)
papers.summary: PAHF (Personalized Agents from Human Feedback) is a continual personalization framework in which a prompted LLM agent learns per-user natural-language preference notes in isolated external memory. It combines proactive pre-action clarification, asked when an instruction is ambiguous and memory lacks relevant information, with reactive post-action feedback that revises memory under preference drift. A four-phase protocol on new embodied-manipulation and online-shopping benchmarks uses simulated personas. PAHF beats No Memory, Pre-action Only and Post-action Only baselines in all phases, and Pre-action Only collapses after drift. Transfer is tested only within a persona, and feedback is simulated and noise-free.
papers.user_evidence: answers to clarifying questions; post-action feedback
papers.relation: Very close to USIL (clarification + memory + feedback); open question is learning a per-user policy for when to ask, not only what to remember.
papers.closest_overlap: PAHF learns per-user memory online from live interaction. It couples pre-action clarification (an ask decision) with post-action feedback to handle drift, and it evaluates across a four-phase longitudinal protocol. This is close to USIL's user-specific history h_t^u and its evolving, sparse evidence. Its sharpest overlap is deciding whether to ask based on what memory already contains.
papers.remaining_question: PAHF's memory stores mostly declarative content preferences and only a one-question ask/no-ask decision. It does not show whether it can learn a per-user procedural policy, such as when a given user wants to be asked, confirmed with, or left alone. Nor does it show whether that policy transfers across users or domains, or holds up with real humans and noisy feedback instead of simulated personas.

papers.title: MemToolAgent: Leveraging Memory for Tool Using Agents Based on Environment and User Feedback
papers.authors: Suleyman Armagan Er, Danilo Ribeiro, Yogesh Virkar, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: A fine-tuning-free memory framework for tool-using agents. It uses a unified memory-entry format and reflection that turns failed executions, together with environment and user feedback, into stored critiques. Retrieval sets how many past experiences to use from the similarity distribution of stored memories. Reports gains on WorkBench, NESTFUL and PEToolBench, including personalized tool use.
papers.user_evidence: User feedback on tool-execution outcomes; environment feedback on failures
papers.relation: Among the closest memory systems to USIL, because it writes user feedback into reusable critiques that change later agent behaviour; open question: whether per-user feedback memories generalize across tasks and shape ask-vs-act decisions, not only tool-call correctness.

papers.title: MultiSessionCollab: Learning User Preferences with Memory to Improve Long-Term Collaboration
papers.authors: Shuhaib Mehri, Priyanka Kargupta, Tal August, Dilek Hakkani-Tür
papers.cite_role: Closest predecessor: multi-session collaboration preferences with memory
papers.summary: MultiSessionCollab is a benchmark for long-term collaboration in which user simulators with personas and three interaction preferences each work with an agent over 20 sessions. The agent keeps a reflective natural-language memory of user preferences, contexts and satisfying strategies, and the reflection policy is trained with GRPO using rewards from simulator behavior. Memory improves task success and reduces user effort and conversation length versus no memory, Mem0 and history baselines, and approaches an oracle. A 19-participant study corroborates the gains but shows weaker cross-domain generalization. Preferences are explicit and static, and ask/act/defer decisions are neither learned nor evaluated.
papers.relation: One of the closest predecessors; remaining question is explicit ask/act/defer decisions and transfer across tasks.
papers.closest_overlap: Each simulated user has three assigned interaction preferences (how the agent should behave), which the agent learns across 20 sessions into a per-user memory that changes later behavior. This is close to procedure_individual learning, and the user-effort metric (preference enforcements) is a procedural evaluation beyond task success [personalization][metrics_and_baselines][temporal_adaptation].
papers.remaining_question: MultiSessionCollab learns what a user prefers but not when to ask, confirm, act or defer, and its preferences are explicit and static. Can a user-conditioned policy learn these decisions from implicit signals such as edits and takeovers under drifting preferences, and transfer to unseen tasks or users?

papers.title: VitaBench 2.0: Evaluating Personalized and Proactive Agents in Long-Term User Interactions
papers.authors: Yuxin Chen, Yi Zhang, Zhengzhou Cai, et al.
papers.cite_role: Evaluation: long-term personalized and proactive agents
papers.summary: VitaBench 2.0 is a benchmark of temporally ordered tool-use task sequences for 56 synthetic users with over 2,000 preferences, three domains (Delivery, In-store, OTA) and 66 tools. Preferences drift between tasks, and histories are fragmented and noisy. Some tasks are proactive, so the agent must ask or explore to fill in missing context. An UPDATE/RETRIEVE memory interface compares full context, agentic memory and RAG across about 25 LLM configurations. The best model reaches Avg@4 of about 0.5 and Pass^4 of about 0.3. Memory usually hurts, performance degrades over the sequence, and proactive scores trail personalization scores. Nothing is trained and transfer is not tested.
papers.what_is_learned: other: evaluation benchmark (memory and user preferences)
papers.user_evidence: Longitudinal per-user interaction histories with scattered, evolving preferences
papers.relation: Combines longitudinal per-user memory with ask-vs-infer evaluation, close to the USIL evaluation setting; open question: does it score whether the agent's asking behaviour adapts to the individual user (asking less once preferences are known), rather than gathering information uniformly?
papers.closest_overlap: VitaBench 2.0 is a longitudinal per-user benchmark with 56 users and 2,000+ preferences, drift events and an UPDATE/RETRIEVE memory interface. It is the closest existing testbed for USIL's evaluation pillar. It also measures proactive asking when context is missing, and finds proactive scores consistently below personalization scores (Claude 27.4 vs 46.0).
papers.remaining_question: The benchmark scores whether the right item is chosen and whether missing information is requested. It does not measure per-user procedural preferences such as how often a given user wants to be asked or confirmed, or when they want to take back control. Can USIL's per-user interaction policies be evaluated on this benchmark, e.g. by adding user-specific ask/confirm tolerances to the restricted simulator, and do they transfer across the three domains?

papers.title: Agent Workflow Memory
papers.authors: Zora Zhiruo Wang, Jiayuan Mao, Daniel Fried, Graham Neubig
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: AWM induces reusable workflows (common sub-routines) from past agent trajectories, offline from training examples or online from test queries, and supplies the relevant ones to guide later actions. Gives 24.6% and 51.1% relative success gains on Mind2Web and WebArena, with growing gains under cross-task, cross-website and cross-domain shift.
papers.user_evidence: None from users directly; the agent's own (self-judged) successful trajectories
papers.decisions_raw: none (it changes which task steps are executed, not ask/act behaviour)
papers.relation: The canonical procedural-memory mechanism, which could hold user-specific routines (which steps a user lets the agent run autonomously); open question: inducing workflows from one user's demonstrations and takeovers, annotated with where the user wants checkpoints.

papers.title: In Prospect and Retrospect: Reflective Memory Management for Long-term Personalized Dialogue Agents
papers.authors: Zhen Tan, Jun Yan, I-Hung Hsu, et al.
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Reflective Memory Management (RMM) builds a personalized memory bank by summarizing interactions at the utterance, turn and session levels (prospective reflection). It then refines retrieval with online RL, using the evidence the LLM cites as the signal (retrospective reflection). Reports more than 10% accuracy gain over a no-memory baseline on LongMemEval.
papers.user_evidence: Multi-session dialogue history; citation signals from the LLM's own responses
papers.relation: Online learning of what to retrieve resembles adapting a per-user memory policy from sparse signals; open question: could the RL signal be real user reactions (accept, edit, interrupt) instead of self-citations, and could it drive interaction decisions?

papers.title: LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory
papers.authors: Di Wu, Hongwei Wang, Wenhao Yu, Yuwei Zhang, Kai-Wei Chang, Dong Yu
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: A 500-question benchmark embedded in scalable user-assistant histories. It tests information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention, and shows about a 30% accuracy drop for commercial assistants and long-context LLMs. Proposes an indexing/retrieval/reading decomposition of memory design with optimizations such as session decomposition and time-aware query expansion.
papers.user_evidence: User-assistant chat histories, including user statements that later update earlier ones
papers.decisions_raw: defer (abstention when the information is not in memory)
papers.relation: The knowledge-update and abstention axes map onto preference drift (P1) and deference (P3), but only for factual recall; open question: does updated memory change downstream interaction choices (for example, stop asking once a preference is known)?

papers.title: Memp: Exploring Agent Procedural Memory
papers.authors: Runnan Fang, Yuan Liang, Xiaobin Wang, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Distills past agent trajectories into a learnable, lifelong procedural memory with step-level instructions and script-like abstractions. Studies strategies for building, retrieving and updating it (including correcting and deprecating outdated entries) and shows gains on TravelPlanner and ALFWorld, plus transfer of memory from stronger to weaker models.
papers.user_evidence: None from users; the agent's own trajectories and task outcomes
papers.relation: Its update, correct and deprecate operations are a template for maintaining evolving procedural preferences under drift; open question: procedural memory keyed to a user, updated from that user's corrections instead of task-success signals.

papers.title: Evaluating Very Long-Term Conversational Memory of LLM Agents
papers.authors: Adyasha Maharana, Dong-Ho Lee, Sergey Tulyakov, Mohit Bansal, Francesco Barbieri, Yuwei Fang
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Introduces LoCoMo: very long multi-session dialogues (about 300 turns and 9K tokens, up to 35 sessions) generated by persona- and event-graph-grounded LLM agents, then human-verified. Benchmarks QA, event summarization and multimodal dialogue generation, and finds that LLMs and RAG lag far behind humans on long-range temporal and causal reasoning.
papers.user_evidence: Long multi-session conversation history (persona facts, temporal events)
papers.relation: The standard longitudinal memory benchmark, but it tests recall of conversational facts rather than whether remembered evidence changes the agent's ask/act behaviour; open question: an analogous long-horizon benchmark whose targets are interaction decisions.

papers.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
papers.authors: Charles Packer, Sarah Wooders, Kevin Lin, et al.
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Proposes virtual context management, inspired by OS memory hierarchies: the LLM manages tiered memory (in-context vs. external) through function calls and interrupts. Evaluated on large-document analysis and multi-session chat, where the agent keeps and builds on user information across sessions.
papers.user_evidence: Multi-session conversation history (facts users state about themselves); no explicit corrections or approvals
papers.decisions_raw: none (the agent decides memory reads and writes, not ask/act choices with the user)
papers.relation: Supplies the architecture for persistent per-user state that a pi_u could condition on, but stores what users said rather than how they want the agent to interact; open question: what memory schema captures interaction-policy evidence such as takeovers and rejections?

papers.title: Collaborative Interface Agents
papers.authors: Yezdi Lashkari; Max Metral; Pattie Maes
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first
papers.summary: Learns patterns from user activity and transfers knowledge across agents; slightly before period
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

papers.title: Getting Better at Working With You: Compiling User Corrections into Runtime Enforcement for Coding Agents
papers.authors: Yujun Zhou, Kehan Guo, Haomin Zhuang, et al. (incl. Nitesh V. Chawla, Xiangliang Zhang)
papers.cite_role: Closest predecessor: user corrections compiled into persistent rules; title overlap
papers.summary: The paper identifies an access-compliance gap in coding agents: they can retrieve a user's remembered corrections and still violate them (compliance is 31.6% with no rules, 55.0% with all rules). Trace, a drop-in skill-layer pipeline, compiles chat corrections into a per-user library of atomic rules, each with an applicability check, a behavior instruction and a verifier. A lifecycle resolver maintains the library, and runtime hooks block task completion until active verifiers pass. On ClawArena and MemoryArena-derived tasks with simulated users, Trace lowers violations and user turns versus Mem0, Hindsight and ReMe-Light. OOD transfer is strong on ClawArena and weak on MemoryArena.
papers.what_is_learned: other: compiled per-user procedural rules / runtime checks
papers.user_evidence: natural-language corrections in chat (anonymized real-user cases)
papers.decisions_raw: act, confirm (gating task completion on user-specific checks)
papers.relation: Very close to USIL's 'tell once' goal for procedural preferences across tasks; open question is whether corrections about the interaction itself (ask less, confirm before X) can be compiled the same way, and how rules are retired when preferences drift.
papers.closest_overlap: Trace is close to procedure_individual: it turns each user's own corrections into a persistent per-user library of procedural rules that gate agent behavior in later sessions, and it measures violation and repeated corrections rather than only task success. It also shows that remembered preferences (Mem0, All Rules) are often not followed.
papers.remaining_question: Trace enforces a fixed rule set as hard gates, so it does not learn when to ask, confirm, defer or hand back control per user. Can per-user rules be turned into a learned, calibrated interaction policy that adapts autonomy and confirmation, and that stays effective as preferences drift in an online setting with real rather than simulated users, given that the evaluation freezes the store and MemoryArena OOD violation stays near 97%?

papers.title: Learning on the Job: Continual Learning from Deployment Feedback for Frozen-Weights Agents
papers.authors: Valentin Tablan, Scott Taylor, Kristoffer Bernhem
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Pairs a frozen LLM agent with an external memory that distills each deployment episode into retrievable natural-language rules, learning from one-bit outcome verdicts or post-hoc corrections; on tau-bench banking, corrections give 2.6x the static-RAG baseline, and memory transfers across models.
papers.user_evidence: outcome verdicts (one-bit) and after-the-fact corrections from operators
papers.relation: Shows continual learning without weight updates from cheap deployment feedback; the memory is shared across users, so per-user scoping and interaction-level rules remain open.

papers.title: SPRInG: Continual LLM Personalization via Selective Parametric Adaptation and Retrieval-Interpolated Generation
papers.authors: Seoyeon Kim, Jaehyung Kim
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Addresses user-interest drift in continual personalization: a likelihood-based novelty score detects genuine preference shifts and updates a user-specific adapter only then (with a replay buffer), and inference interpolates parametric outputs with gated retrieval over history.
papers.user_evidence: stream of a user's historical interactions/documents
papers.relation: Directly tackles separating real drift from transient context in per-user continual updates; open question is whether drift-gated updates work for interaction-policy evidence, which is sparser and noisier.

papers.title: Principled Fine-tuning of LLMs from User-Edits: A Medley of Preference, Supervision, and Reward
papers.authors: Dipendra Misra, Aldo Pacchiano, Ta-Chung Chi, Ge Gao
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Treats deployment logs of (context, agent response, user edit) as a mix of preference, supervised, and cost feedback; derives learning bounds for each and proposes an ensembling procedure that learns from all three, adapting robustly to different user-edit distributions at test time (domains adapted from PRELUDE).
papers.user_evidence: user edits to agent responses in writing-assistant settings
papers.relation: Gives the theory for learning from edits, a core USIL evidence type; open question is whether edit cost can also train interaction decisions (for example, confirm before acting when expected edit cost is high).

papers.title: Retrospective Learning from Interactions
papers.authors: Zizhao Chen, Mustafa Omer Gul, Yiwei Chen, Gloria Geng, Anne Wu, Yoav Artzi
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Shows that implicit signals in multi-turn deployed interactions (rephrasing, frustration, switching tasks) are task-general and can be decoded retrospectively into rewards; ReSpect retrains the model over successive deployment rounds with thousands of real human interactions, raising task completion from 31% to 82%.
papers.user_evidence: implicit conversational feedback in follow-up turns (rephrasings, approval/frustration, task abandonment) during live deployment
papers.decisions_raw: none (task actions improved; no ask/act/defer modeled)
papers.relation: Closest working example of continual learning from implicit in-deployment evidence; open question is whether the same retrospective decoding can be kept per user and applied to interaction decisions (e.g., when the user rephrases because the agent should have asked).

papers.title: Right Now, Wrong Then: Non-Stationary Direct Preference Optimization under Preference Drift
papers.authors: Seongho Son, William Bankes, Sayak Ray Chowdhury, Brooks Paige, Ilija Bogunovic
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Models time-varying preferences with a Dynamic Bradley-Terry model and proposes NS-DPO, which exponentially discounts older preference pairs; gives estimation-error and regret bounds under unknown drift and shows robustness when fine-tuning LLMs under drifting preferences.
papers.relation: Gives a principled discounting approach for drift in preference evidence; open question is how to discount sparse per-user interaction evidence (e.g., takeovers) and tell real drift from context-dependent variation.

papers.title: The Era of Real-World Human Interaction: RL from User Conversations
papers.authors: Chuanyang Jin, Jing Xu, Bo Liu, et al. (incl. Tianmin Shu, Jason Weston)
papers.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2509.25137 (also an ICLR 2026 workshop poster)
papers.cite_role: map core: cite in appendix / extended related work
papers.summary: Proposes Reinforcement Learning from Human Interaction (RLHI), which learns from organic WildChat conversations through (i) user-guided rewrites that revise weak outputs using the user's follow-up message and (ii) persona-conditioned rewards built from each user's long-term interaction history; improves personalization and instruction following.
papers.user_evidence: natural follow-up messages (corrections, complaints, requests) and long-term per-user conversation history summarized as a persona
papers.relation: Conditions a reward on each user's multi-session history built from natural follow-ups; it still learns output preferences rather than when to ask, confirm, or defer for that user.

papers.title: Personalized Adaptation via In-Context Preference Learning
papers.authors: Allison Lau, Younwoo Choi, Vahid Balazadeh, Keertana Chidambaram, Vasilis Syrgkanis, Rahul G. Krishnan
papers.venue: NeurIPS 2024 Workshop on Adaptive Foundation Models; arXiv preprint arXiv:2410.14001
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Preference Pretrained Transformer (PPT) is trained offline with a history-dependent loss so that, online, it adapts to an individual user's preferences purely in context from that user's feedback; it outperforms per-user fine-tuning baselines in a contextual-bandit setting at much lower compute.
papers.user_evidence: online per-user preference feedback accumulated in context
papers.relation: A test-time adaptation recipe (meta-train offline, adapt in context) that could carry over to learning pi_u; still open whether it scales beyond bandit toys to multi-step interaction decisions.

papers.title: Robot Learning on the Job: Human-in-the-Loop Autonomy and Learning During Deployment
papers.authors: Huihan Liu, Soroush Nasiriany, Lance Zhang, Zhiyao Bao, Yuke Zhu
papers.venue: Robotics: Science and Systems (RSS) 2023; arXiv preprint arXiv:2211.08416
papers.cite_role: map only
papers.summary: Sirius: a partially autonomous robot runs while a human monitors and takes over at hard moments; deployment data are reweighted by estimated human trust (from interventions) and used for weighted behavior cloning, improving the policy across deployment rounds.
papers.user_evidence: human takeovers/interventions and corrective demonstrations during deployment
papers.decisions_raw: act, defer (via human intervention; autonomy share grows over rounds)
papers.relation: A foundational example of turning takeovers into learning signal and gradually shifting autonomy; open question is how to make this per user, since takeovers reflect individual trust and preference as well as policy failure.

papers.title: Physical interaction as communication: Learning robot objectives online from human corrections
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first
papers.summary: Learns user task objectives online from corrections; useful distinction from learning procedure
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P2; capabilities require full-text verification.

papers.title: Learning from interventions: Human-robot interaction as both explicit and implicit feedback
papers.cite_role: candidate: verify with the pipeline first
papers.summary: Treats interventions and non-interventions as evidence for robot learning
papers.relation: Candidate historical/adjacent work relevant to P1;P3; capabilities require full-text verification.
